Definition 13 (Conditional precision) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\) be a \(p \times 1\) multivariate Gaussian vector, and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-i}\) be \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\) without its \(i\)th element. The conditional precision of \(X_i\) given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-i} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-i}\) is the precision computed from the conditional variance of \(X_i\) given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-i} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-i}\):

\[ \tau\mathopen{}\left(X_i \mid \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-i} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-i}\right)\mathclose{} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left({{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X_i \mid\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-i} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-i}\right)\mathclose{}}}\right)\mathclose{}}^{-1}. \]

ExmExample 22 (The conditional precision of one element of a bivariate Gaussian vector)

Example 22 (The conditional precision of one element of a bivariate Gaussian vector)  

Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}= {(X_1, X_2)}^{\top} \sim \operatorname{N}_2\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{0}, \begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}\right)\mathclose{}\) with \(\mathopen{}\left|\rho\right|\mathclose{} < 1\). By Example 21, \(X_1\) given \(X_2 = x_2\) has variance \(1 - \rho^2\), so the conditional precision of \(X_1\) given \(X_2 = x_2\) is

\[ \frac{1}{1 - \rho^2}. \]

DefDefinition 14 (Coprecision)

Definition 14 (Coprecision) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\) be a \(p \times 1\) multivariate Gaussian vector with \(p \ge 2\), let \(i \ne j\), and let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij}\) be \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\) without its \(i\)th and \(j\)th elements. The coprecision of \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\) is defined through their conditional covariance and their conditional variances as

\[ \frac{-{{\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_j \mid\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\right)\mathclose{}}}} {{{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X_i \mid\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\right)\mathclose{}}}{{\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X_j \mid\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\right)\mathclose{}}} - \mathopen{}\left({{\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_i, X_j \mid\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\right)\mathclose{}}}\right)\mathclose{}^2}. \]

ExmExample 23 (The coprecision of a bivariate Gaussian vector)

Example 23 (The coprecision of a bivariate Gaussian vector)  

Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}= {(X_1, X_2)}^{\top} \sim \operatorname{N}_2\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{0}, \begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}\right)\mathclose{}\) with \(\mathopen{}\left|\rho\right|\mathclose{} < 1\). With no other elements to condition on, the conditional variances of \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are both 1 and their conditional covariance is \(\rho\), so the coprecision of \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) is

\[ \frac{-\rho}{1 \cdot 1 - \rho^2} = \frac{-\rho}{1 - \rho^2}. \]

DefDefinition 15 (Precision matrix)

Definition 15 (Precision matrix) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\) be a \(p \times 1\) multivariate Gaussian vector. The precision matrix \(\tau(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}})\) of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\) is the \(p \times p\) matrix whose \(i\)th diagonal element is the conditional precision of \(X_i\) given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-i}\), and whose \((i, j)\) element, for \(i \ne j\), is the coprecision of \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij}\).

LemTheorem 20 (The precision matrix is the inverse of the variance matrix)

Theorem 20 (The precision matrix is the inverse of the variance matrix) If \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\) has the multivariate normal distribution \(\operatorname{N}_p\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}}, \mathbf{\Sigma}\right)\mathclose{}\), then \(\tau(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}) = {\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}\right)\mathclose{}}^{-1}\).

ProofProof

Proof. Let \(\mathbf{\Omega} = {\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{\Sigma}\right)\mathclose{}}^{-1}\). Reordering the elements of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\) reorders the rows and columns of \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\) and of \(\mathbf{\Omega}\) in the same way, so for each \(i\) and \(j\) we may take \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) to be the last two elements.

Cut \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\) into blocks with the first \(p - 2\) elements in the first block. By the inverse of a positive definite block matrix, the last \(2 \times 2\) block of \(\mathbf{\Omega}\) is \({\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{S}\right)\mathclose{}}^{-1}\), where \(\mathbf{S}\) is the Schur complement of the first block of \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\). By Theorem 19, \(\mathbf{S}\) is the variance matrix of \({(X_i, X_j)}^{\top}\) given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\), so the diagonal elements \(v_i\) and \(v_j\) of \(\mathbf{S}\) are the conditional variances of \(X_i\) and \(X_j\), and its off-diagonal element \(c_{ij}\) is their conditional covariance. The inverse of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix gives the off-diagonal element of \(\mathbf{\Omega}\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{\Omega}_{ij} &= \mathopen{}\left({\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{S}\right)\mathclose{}}^{-1}\right)\mathclose{}_{12} && \text{(last block of } \mathbf{\Omega} \text{)} \\ &= \frac{-c_{ij}}{v_i v_j - c_{ij}^2} && \text{(inverse of a } 2 \times 2 \text{ matrix)} \end{aligned} \]

which is the coprecision of \(X_i\) and \(X_j\).

Taking \(X_i\) alone as the last element, the last \(1 \times 1\) block of \(\mathbf{\Omega}\) is \({\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{S}\right)\mathclose{}}^{-1}\), where by Theorem 19 \(\mathbf{S}\) is the conditional variance of \(X_i\) given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-i} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-i}\). So \(\mathbf{\Omega}_{ii}\) is the inverse of that conditional variance, which is the conditional precision of \(X_i\).

ExmExample 24 (The precision matrix of a bivariate Gaussian vector)

Example 24 (The precision matrix of a bivariate Gaussian vector)  

Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}= {(X_1, X_2)}^{\top} \sim \operatorname{N}_2\mathopen{}\left(\mathbf{0}, \begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}\right)\mathclose{}\) with \(\mathopen{}\left|\rho\right|\mathclose{} < 1\). By Example 22 and Example 23, the conditional precision of each element is \(1 / (1 - \rho^2)\), and the coprecision of \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) is \(-\rho / (1 - \rho^2)\), so

\[ \tau(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}) = \frac{1}{1 - \rho^2} \begin{pmatrix}1 & -\rho \\ -\rho & 1\end{pmatrix}. \]

This matrix is the inverse of \(\begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}\), as the precision matrix is the inverse of the variance matrix says, because

\[ \begin{aligned} \begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \rho^2} \begin{pmatrix}1 & -\rho \\ -\rho & 1\end{pmatrix} &= \frac{1}{1 - \rho^2} \begin{pmatrix}1 - \rho^2 & -\rho + \rho \\ \rho - \rho & -\rho^2 + 1\end{pmatrix} \\ &= \mathbf{I}_2. \end{aligned} \]

LemTheorem 21 (A zero off-diagonal element of the precision matrix means conditional independence)

Theorem 21 (A zero off-diagonal element of the precision matrix means conditional independence) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\sim \operatorname{N}_p\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}}, \mathbf{\Sigma}\right)\mathclose{}\) with \(p \ge 2\), and let \(i \ne j\). The \((i, j)\) element of the precision matrix \(\tau(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}})\) is zero if and only if \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) are conditionally independent given the continuous random vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij}\), that is, \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\) without its \(i\)th and \(j\)th elements.

ProofProof

Proof. By Theorem 20, the \((i, j)\) element of \(\tau(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}})\) is the coprecision of \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\). Write \(v_i\) and \(v_j\) for the conditional variances of \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\), and \(c_{ij}\) for their conditional covariance. By Theorem 19, given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\), \({(X_i, X_j)}^{\top}\) has a bivariate Gaussian distribution whose variance matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) is positive definite, with diagonal elements \(v_i\) and \(v_j\) and off-diagonal element \(c_{ij}\), and \(\mathbf{S}\) does not depend on \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\). A positive definite matrix has a positive determinant, so \(v_i v_j - c_{ij}^2 > 0\), and the coprecision \(-c_{ij} / (v_i v_j - c_{ij}^2)\) is zero exactly when \(c_{ij} = 0\).

If \(c_{ij} = 0\), then \(\mathbf{S}\) is diagonal, so by Corollary 7 \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) are independent given \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\), for every \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\). That is, the conditional density of \({(X_i, X_j)}^{\top}\) equals the conditional density of \(X_i\) times the conditional density of \(X_j\), which is the factorization in the definition of conditional independence. Conversely, if \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) are conditionally independent, then they are independent given each \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}_{-ij} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}_{-ij}\), so by Corollary 7 \(c_{ij} = 0\).

ExmExample 25 (A chain of three Gaussian variables)

Example 25 (A chain of three Gaussian variables)  

Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}= {(X_1, X_2, X_3)}^{\top}\) have \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\right]\mathclose{}} = \mathbf{0}\) and precision matrix

\[ \tau(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}) = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}. \]

By Theorem 20, the variance matrix is the inverse of this matrix,

\[ {\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{X}}\vphantom{X}}\right)\mathclose{}} = \frac{1}{4} \begin{pmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}, \]

which one can check by multiplying the two matrices to get \(\mathbf{I}_3\). So \({\operatorname{Cov}\mathopen{}\left(X_1, X_3\right)\mathclose{}} = 1/4 \ne 0\), and \(X_1\) and \(X_3\) are not independent. But the \((1, 3)\) element of the precision matrix is 0, so by Theorem 21, \(X_1\) and \(X_3\) are conditionally independent given \(X_2\): once \(X_2\) is known, \(X_1\) carries no further information about \(X_3\).

LemTheorem 22 (Mahalanobis distance in eigenvector coordinates)

Theorem 22 (Mahalanobis distance in eigenvector coordinates) Let \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\) be positive definite, with eigendecomposition \(\mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{\Lambda}{\mathbf{Q}}^{\top}\), where \(\mathbf{Q}\) has columns \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_1, \ldots, \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_p\) and \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) has diagonal elements \(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p\). Then:

\[ \Delta(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^p\frac{\mathopen{}\left({\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_i}^{\top}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}})\right)\mathclose{}^2}{\lambda_i} \]

ProofProof

Proof. Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} = {\mathbf{Q}}^{\top}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}})\), whose \(i\)-th element is \(y_i = {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_i}^{\top}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}})\). By the inverse of a positive definite matrix, \(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{\Lambda}^{-1}{\mathbf{Q}}^{\top}\), with every \(\lambda_i > 0\). So:

\[ \begin{aligned} \Delta(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})^2 &= {(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}})}^{\top} \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{\Lambda}^{-1}{\mathbf{Q}}^{\top} (\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}}) && \text{(definition; substitute } \mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1} \text{)} \\ &= {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}^{\top} \mathbf{\Lambda}^{-1} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}} && \text{(} {(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}})}^{\top}\mathbf{Q} = {\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{y}}\vphantom{y}}}^{\top} \text{)} \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^p\frac{y_i^2}{\lambda_i} && \text{(} \mathbf{\Lambda}^{-1} \text{ is diagonal)} \end{aligned} \]

RemarkRemark

Remark. \(y_i\) is the coordinate of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}- \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}}\) along the eigenvector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_i\). So the set of points at Mahalanobis distance \(\delta\) from \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}}\), where the multivariate normal density is constant (Corollary 6), is an ellipse (\(p = 2\)) or ellipsoid centered at \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}}\), with axes along the eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\) and half-length \(\delta\sqrt{\lambda_i}\) along \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_i\).

ExmExample 26 (Elliptical contours of a bivariate normal density)

Example 26 (Elliptical contours of a bivariate normal density) Let \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\mu}}\vphantom{\mu}} = \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}\) and \(\mathbf{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\), which has eigenvalues \(3\) and \(1\), with eigenvectors \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{(1, 1)}^{\top}\) and \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{(1, -1)}^{\top}\) (an eigendecomposition example). By Theorem 22:

\[ \Delta(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})^2 = \frac{(x_1 + x_2)^2}{2 \cdot 3} + \frac{(x_1 - x_2)^2}{2 \cdot 1} \]

The point

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}&= \sqrt{3}\,\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_1 \\ &= \sqrt{3/2}\,{(1, 1)}^{\top} \end{aligned} \]

has \(x_1 + x_2 = \sqrt{6}\) and \(x_1 - x_2 = 0\), so

\[ \begin{aligned} \Delta(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})^2 &= 6/6 \\ &= 1; \end{aligned} \]

the point \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}= \mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{q}}\vphantom{q}}_2\) has \(x_1 + x_2 = 0\) and \(x_1 - x_2 = \sqrt{2}\), so

\[ \begin{aligned} \Delta(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}})^2 &= 2/2 \\ &= 1. \end{aligned} \]

So the contour \(\Delta(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{x}}\vphantom{x}}) = 1\) of the \(\operatorname{N}_2\mathopen{}\left(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{0}}\vphantom{0}}, \mathbf{\Sigma}\right)\mathclose{}\) density is an ellipse stretched along \({(1, 1)}^{\top}\), with half-length \(\sqrt{3}\), and squeezed along \({(1, -1)}^{\top}\), with half-length \(1\): \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are positively correlated (Figure 6).

Show code 
# The covariance matrix of the example and its eigendecomposition.
mh_entries <- c(2, 1, 1, 2)
mh_covmat <- matrix(mh_entries, nrow = 2)
mh_eig <- eigen(mh_covmat)
mh_values <- mh_eig$values
mh_expected <- c(3, 1)
mh_matches <- all.equal(mh_values, mh_expected)
stopifnot(mh_matches)

# The Mahalanobis distance of each grid point from the mean zero.
mh_axis <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 200)
mh_grid <- tidyr::expand_grid(x1 = mh_axis, x2 = mh_axis)
mh_points <- as.matrix(mh_grid)
mh_inverse <- solve(mh_covmat)
mh_quad <- (mh_points %*% mh_inverse) * mh_points
mh_sums <- rowSums(mh_quad)
mh_dist <- sqrt(mh_sums)
mh_grid <- dplyr::mutate(mh_grid, mahal = mh_dist)

# The points of the example: sqrt(3) q1 and q2, each at distance 1.
mh_long <- sqrt(3 / 2)
mh_short <- 1 / sqrt(2)
mh_marks_x1 <- c(mh_long, mh_short)
mh_marks_x2 <- c(mh_long, -mh_short)
mh_marks <- tibble::tibble(x1 = mh_marks_x1, x2 = mh_marks_x2)

mh_contour_aes <- ggplot2::aes(z = mahal, colour = ggplot2::after_stat(level))
mh_breaks <- c(1, 2)
mh_contours <- ggplot2::geom_contour(mh_contour_aes, breaks = mh_breaks)
mh_dots <- ggplot2::geom_point(data = mh_marks, size = 2.5)
mh_colours <- ggplot2::scale_colour_viridis_c(
  name = "Mahalanobis distance",
  end = 0.7,
  breaks = mh_breaks,
  guide = "legend"
)
mh_plot <- mh_grid |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::aes(x1, x2) +
  mh_contours +
  mh_dots +
  mh_colours +
  ggplot2::coord_fixed(expand = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "x1", y = "x2") +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")

mh_is_html <- knitr::is_html_output()
if (mh_is_html) {
  mh_legend <- list(
    orientation = "h",
    x = 0.5,
    xanchor = "center",
    y = -0.25
  )
  mh_widget <- plotly::ggplotly(mh_plot) |>
    plotly::layout(legend = mh_legend) |>
    plotly::config(displaylogo = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
  htmltools::div(
    role = "img",
    `aria-label` = fig_alt_mahal_eigen,
    mh_widget
  )
} else {
  mh_plot
}

LemTheorem 23 (The maximum of the Gaussian density)

Theorem 23 (The maximum of the Gaussian density) If \(X \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(\mu, \sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\) (Gaussian distribution), then its density is largest at \(x = \mu\), where it equals:

\[\max_x \mathbb{p}(X=x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\]

ProofProof

Proof. For each \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), the quantity \(u(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}(x-\mu)^2 / (2\sigma^2)\) is at least \(0\), and it equals \(0\) only at \(x = \mu\). The factor \(\text{e}^{-u(x)}\) of the density is at most \(1\):

\[ \begin{aligned} -u(x) &\le 0 && \text{(a square is non-negative, and } 2\sigma^2> 0 \text{)} \\ \text{e}^{-u(x)} &\le \text{e}^{0} && \text{(} \text{e}^t \text{ is increasing in } t \text{)} \\ &= 1 && \text{(} \text{e}^0 = 1 \text{)} \end{aligned} \]

Multiplying both sides by \(1 / (\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}) > 0\) keeps their order:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{p}(X=x) &= \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-u(x)} && \text{(Gaussian density)} \\ &\le \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} && \text{(} \text{e}^{-u(x)} \le 1 \text{)} \end{aligned} \]

Equality holds at \(x = \mu\), where \(u(x) = 0\), so the density peaks there.

ExmExample 27 (The peak of the Gaussian density grows as the standard deviation shrinks)

Example 27 (The peak of the Gaussian density grows as the standard deviation shrinks) By Theorem 23, the peak of the density of \({\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(0, \sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\) is \(1 / (\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})\). Figure 8 marks each peak for standard deviations \(0.5\), \(1\) and \(2\).

Show code 
sds <- c(0.5, 1, 2)
x_grid <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 400)
sd_label <- latex2exp::TeX("$\\sigma$")
density_label <- latex2exp::TeX("$f(x)$")

normal_curves <-
  dplyr::tibble(sd = sds) |>
  dplyr::reframe(.by = sd, x = x_grid) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    density = dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = sd),
    sd = factor(sd)
  )

normal_peaks <-
  dplyr::tibble(sd = sds) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    peak = 1 / (sd * sqrt(2 * pi)),
    sd = factor(sd)
  )

normal_plot <-
  normal_curves |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = density, col = sd) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = normal_peaks,
    ggplot2::aes(x = 0, y = peak)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(col = sd_label, y = density_label) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")

print(normal_plot)

As \(\sigma \to 0\), the peak \(1 / (\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})\) grows indefinitely, so a density can exceed \(1\).

LemTheorem 24 (Gaussian distributions are closed under affine transformations)

Theorem 24 (Gaussian distributions are closed under affine transformations) If \(X \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(\mu, \sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\) and \(a \ne 0\), then \(aX + b \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(a\mu+ b, a^2\sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\).

ProofProof

Proof. Let \(Y = aX + b\). Let \(f\) be the density of \(X\). The CDF of \(Y\) is \(\mathbb{F}_Y\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{} = \Pr(aX + b \le y)\). The density \(f\) is continuous everywhere. So at every \(y\), the derivative of \(\mathbb{F}_Y\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{}\) is the density of \(Y\), by the derivative of the CDF is the density. To differentiate \(\mathbb{F}_Y\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{}\), write it through the CDF \(\mathbb{F}_X\) of \(X\). There are two cases, by the sign of \(a\).

  • Case \(a > 0\). Dividing by \(a > 0\) leaves \(\le\) as \(\le\), so:

    \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{F}_Y\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{} &= {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(X \le \frac{y-b}{a}\right)\mathclose{}} && \text{(} aX + b \le y \iff X \le (y-b)/a \text{)} \\ &= \mathbb{F}_X\mathopen{}\left(\frac{y-b}{a}\right)\mathclose{} && \text{(definition of the CDF)} \end{aligned} \]

    The chain rule gives the derivative:

    \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \mathbb{F}_Y\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{} = \frac{1}{a} f\mathopen{}\left(\frac{y-b}{a}\right)\mathclose{} = \frac{1}{\mathopen{}\left|a\right|\mathclose{}} f\mathopen{}\left(\frac{y-b}{a}\right)\mathclose{} \quad \text{(} \mathopen{}\left|a\right|\mathclose{} = a \text{)} \]

  • Case \(a < 0\). Dividing by \(a < 0\) turns \(\le\) into \(\ge\), and \(\Pr(X = x) = 0\) for a continuous random variable \(X\), so:

    \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{F}_Y\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{} &= {\Pr\mathopen{}\left(X \ge \frac{y-b}{a}\right)\mathclose{}} && \text{(} aX + b \le y \iff X \ge (y-b)/a \text{)} \\ &= 1 - \mathbb{F}_X\mathopen{}\left(\frac{y-b}{a}\right)\mathclose{} && \text{(complement, and } \Pr(X = (y-b)/a) = 0 \text{)} \end{aligned} \]

    The chain rule gives the derivative:

    \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \mathbb{F}_Y\mathopen{}\left(y\right)\mathclose{} = -\frac{1}{a} f\mathopen{}\left(\frac{y-b}{a}\right)\mathclose{} = \frac{1}{\mathopen{}\left|a\right|\mathclose{}} f\mathopen{}\left(\frac{y-b}{a}\right)\mathclose{} \quad \text{(} \mathopen{}\left|a\right|\mathclose{} = -a \text{)} \]

In both cases, \(Y\) has density \(\mathbb{p}(Y=y) = f\mathopen{}\left((y-b)/a\right)\mathclose{} / \mathopen{}\left|a\right|\mathclose{}\). Substitute the Gaussian density of \(X\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{p}(Y=y) &= \frac{1}{\mathopen{}\left|a\right|\mathclose{}} \cdot\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-\frac{\mathopen{}\left((y-b)/a - \mu\right)\mathclose{}^2}{2\sigma^2}} && \text{(Gaussian density of } X \text{)} \\ &= \frac{1}{\mathopen{}\left|a\right|\mathclose{}\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-\frac{\mathopen{}\left((y-b-a\mu)/a\right)\mathclose{}^2}{2\sigma^2}} && \text{(common denominator } a \text{)} \\ &= \frac{1}{\mathopen{}\left|a\right|\mathclose{}\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-\frac{(y-(a\mu+b))^2}{2a^2\sigma^2}} && \text{(} (u/a)^2 = u^2/a^2 \text{)} \\ &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2\sigma^2}\sqrt{2\pi}} \text{e}^{-\frac{(y-(a\mu+b))^2}{2a^2\sigma^2}} && \text{(} \mathopen{}\left|a\right|\mathclose{}\sigma= \sqrt{a^2\sigma^2} \text{)} \end{aligned} \]

The last line is the density of \({\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(a\mu+ b, a^2\sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\) because \(a^2\sigma^2> 0\).

ExmExample 28 (Standardizing a Gaussian random variable)

Example 28 (Standardizing a Gaussian random variable)  

Let \(X \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(\mu, \sigma^2\right)\mathclose{}}\) with \(\sigma> 0\), and let \(Z = (X - \mu) / \sigma\). Then \(Z = aX + b\) with \(a = 1 / \sigma\) and \(b = -\mu/ \sigma\), and \(a \ne 0\). By Theorem 24, \(Z\) is Gaussian with parameters:

\[ \begin{aligned} a\mu+ b &= \frac{\mu}{\sigma} - \frac{\mu}{\sigma} && \text{(substitute } a \text{ and } b \text{)} \\ &= 0 && \text{(} u - u = 0 \text{)} \\ a^2\sigma^2 &= \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2} && \text{(} a^2 = 1/\sigma^2\text{)} \\ &= 1 && \text{(} u/u = 1 \text{)} \end{aligned} \]

So \(Z \sim {\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(0, 1\right)\mathclose{}}\).

9 Mixture distributions

DefDefinition 16 (Mixture density)

Definition 16 (Mixture density) Let \({\mathbb{p}_1}, \ldots, {\mathbb{p}_K}\) be densities on \(\mathbb{R}\), and let \(w_1, \ldots, w_K\) be numbers with:

  • \(w_c \ge 0\) for every \(c\), and
  • \(\sum_{c=1}^{K} w_c = 1\).

The mixture of \({\mathbb{p}_1}, \ldots, {\mathbb{p}_K}\) with mixing weights \(w_1, \ldots, w_K\) is the function [9]:

\[ {\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(x) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\sum_{c=1}^{K} w_c \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x), \quad x \in \mathbb{R} \]

DefDefinition 17 (Mixture component)

Definition 17 (Mixture component) The densities \({\mathbb{p}_1}, \ldots, {\mathbb{p}_K}\) in a mixture (Definition 16) are its components.

LemTheorem 25 (A mixture is the density of a two-stage random variable)

Theorem 25 (A mixture is the density of a two-stage random variable) Let \(C\) be a discrete random variable and \(X\) a continuous random variable with joint density-mass function

\[\mathbb{p}(C = c,\, X = x) = w_c \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x), \quad c \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, K\right\}\mathclose{}},\]

with \({\mathbb{p}_c}\) and \(w_c\) as in Definition 16. Then:

  • \(\mathbb{P}(C = c) = w_c\),
  • for each \(c\) with \(w_c > 0\), the conditional density of \(X\) given \(C = c\) is \({\mathbb{p}_c}\), and
  • the mixture \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}\) is a density of \(X\).
ProofProof

Proof. By the marginal PMF from a joint density-mass function,

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(C = c) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} w_c \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x)\,dx \\ &= w_c, \end{aligned} \]

because \({\mathbb{p}_c}\) is a density and so integrates to 1. Then, by the definition of the conditional density,

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{p}(X = x \mid C = c) &= w_c \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x) / w_c \\ &= {\mathbb{p}_c}(x). \end{aligned} \]

For the last claim, the events \({\mathopen{}\left\{C = 1\right\}\mathclose{}}, \ldots, {\mathopen{}\left\{C = K\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are mutually exclusive, and their union is the whole sample space. So for any interval \(B\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \Pr(X \in B) &= \sum_{c=1}^{K} \Pr(C = c,\, X \in B) && \text{(additivity over the events } {\mathopen{}\left\{C = c\right\}\mathclose{}} \text{)} \\ &= \sum_{c=1}^{K} \int_B w_c \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x)\,dx && \text{(definition of a joint density-mass function)} \\ &= \int_B \sum_{c=1}^{K} w_c \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x)\,dx && \text{(a finite sum of integrals is the integral of the sum)} \\ &= \int_B {\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(x)\,dx && \text{(definition of a mixture)} \end{aligned} \]

And \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}} \ge 0\), as a sum of non-negative terms, so \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}\) is a density of \(X\).

RemarkRemark

Remark. Theorem 25 describes how to generate a draw from a mixture: first draw a component label \(C\) with \(\mathbb{P}(C = c) = w_c\), then draw \(X\) from the component density \({\mathbb{p}_C}\). In applications, \(C\) is often an unobserved subpopulation, such as a disease subtype. Mixtures of multivariate densities, such as mixtures of multivariate normal densities (Gaussian mixture models), work the same way, with \(p\)-variable densities in place of densities on \(\mathbb{R}\).

LemTheorem 26 (The mean of a mixture is the weighted mean of the component means)

Theorem 26 (The mean of a mixture is the weighted mean of the component means) If \(X\) has density \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}\) (Definition 16), and each component \({\mathbb{p}_c}\) has a defined mean \(\mu_c = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x)\,dx\), then:

\[{\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[X\right]\mathclose{}} = \sum_{c=1}^{K} w_c \, \mu_c\]

ProofProof

Proof. The integral defining \({\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[X\right]\mathclose{}}\) converges absolutely, because \(\int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathopen{}\left|x\right|\mathclose{} \, {\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(x)\,dx = \sum_{c=1}^{K} w_c \int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathopen{}\left|x\right|\mathclose{} \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x)\,dx\), a finite sum of finite numbers. Then:

\[ \begin{aligned} {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[X\right]\mathclose{}} &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, {\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(x)\,dx && \text{(definition of expectation)} \\ &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \sum_{c=1}^{K} w_c \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x)\,dx && \text{(definition of a mixture)} \\ &= \sum_{c=1}^{K} w_c \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x)\,dx && \text{(a finite sum of integrals is the integral of the sum)} \\ &= \sum_{c=1}^{K} w_c \, \mu_c && \text{(definition of } \mu_c \text{)} \end{aligned} \]

The first step is the definition of expectation.

LemTheorem 27 (Which component did an observation come from?)

Theorem 27 (Which component did an observation come from?) Under the conditions of Theorem 25, for each \(x\) with \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(x) > 0\):

\[ \mathbb{P}(C = c \mid X = x) = \frac{w_c \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k \, {\mathbb{p}_k}(x)} \]

ProofProof

Proof. By Theorem 25, \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}\) is a density of \(X\). By the definition of the conditional PMF (the case \(X\) continuous, \(C\) discrete):

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(C = c \mid X = x) &= \frac{\mathbb{p}(C = c,\, X = x)}{\mathbb{p}(X = x)} && \text{(definition of the conditional PMF)} \\ &= \frac{w_c \, {\mathbb{p}_c}(x)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k \, {\mathbb{p}_k}(x)} && \text{(substitute the joint density-mass function and } {\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}} \text{)} \end{aligned} \]

RemarkRemark

Remark. Theorem 27 has the form of Bayes’ theorem, with densities in place of some probabilities: the prior probability \(w_c\) of component \(c\) is multiplied by the component density \({\mathbb{p}_c}(x)\) at the observation and divided by the overall density \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(x)\), which plays the role of the law of total probability.

DefDefinition 18 (Responsibility of a mixture component)

Definition 18 (Responsibility of a mixture component) In the setting of Theorem 27, the conditional probability \(\mathbb{P}(C = c \mid X = x)\) is called, in machine learning, the responsibility of component \(c\) for \(x\).

ExmExample 29 (A two-component normal mixture)

Example 29 (A two-component normal mixture) Let \({\mathbb{p}_1}\) be the \({\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(0, 1\right)\mathclose{}}\) density and \({\mathbb{p}_2}\) the \({\operatorname{N}\mathopen{}\left(6, 1\right)\mathclose{}}\) density, with mixing weights \(w_1 = 0.3\) and \(w_2 = 0.7\), and let \(X\) have density \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}} = 0.3\,{\mathbb{p}_1} + 0.7\,{\mathbb{p}_2}\).

  • Mean. By Theorem 26 and the normal means,

    \[ \begin{aligned} {\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\left[X\right]\mathclose{}} &= 0.3 \cdot 0 + 0.7 \cdot 6 \\ &= 4.2. \end{aligned} \]

  • Density. \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}\) has peaks near the two component means, \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(0) \approx 0.120\) and \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(6) \approx 0.279\), with a trough between them, \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(3) \approx 0.004\). The density at the mean, \({\mathbb{p}_{\text{mix}}}(4.2) \approx 0.055\), is less than half its value at either peak.

  • Responsibilities. By Theorem 27, at \(x = 3\), halfway between the component means, \({\mathbb{p}_1}(3) = {\mathbb{p}_2}(3)\) by the symmetry of the normal density, so:

    \[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{P}(C = 2 \mid X = 3) &= \frac{0.7\,{\mathbb{p}_2}(3)}{0.3\,{\mathbb{p}_1}(3) + 0.7\,{\mathbb{p}_2}(3)} \\ &= \frac{0.7}{0.3 + 0.7} \\ &= 0.7, \end{aligned} \]

    the prior weight: an observation equally far from both components carries no information about which component it came from. At \(x = 4.2\), the same formula gives \(\mathbb{P}(C = 2 \mid X = 4.2) \approx 0.9997\).

RemarkRemark

Remark. Example 29 shows that the mean of a mixture can fall where observations are rare, so a single normal distribution fitted to such data would describe them poorly.

ExmExample 30 (The negative binomial as a continuous mixture)

Example 30 (The negative binomial as a continuous mixture) The negative binomial distribution is a mixture of Poisson distributions with a continuum of components, one for each mean \({\lambda}> 0\): its PMF is \(\mathbb{P}(Y = y) = \int_0^\infty g({\lambda})\,\frac{{\lambda}^y e^{-{\lambda}}}{y!}\,d{\lambda}\), where the gamma density \(g\) plays the role of the mixing weights and the integral replaces the sum in Definition 16 (see the proof of Theorem 11).

ExrExercise 4 (Choosing a family for a research question)

Exercise 4 (Choosing a family for a research question) A clinic wants to describe the number of emergency visits it receives each week. Which of the families named on this page fits this research question, and why?

SolutionSolution 2

Solution 2. A weekly visit count is a non-negative whole number with no largest value. The Poisson distribution is a natural first choice for such a count, because its values are \(0, 1, 2, \ldots\). A Bernoulli variable takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\), and a Gaussian count can be negative or fractional, so neither matches the weekly count.

If the weekly counts vary more than a Poisson count allows, the negative binomial distribution is the next candidate.

10 Distribution functions in R

R names its functions by a prefix that says what the function computes, followed by a short name for the family (Table 4 and Table 5).

R has no separate Bernoulli family: use the binomial functions with size = 1. The next chunk evaluates each prefix for the standard Gaussian distribution and for a binomial distribution with three trials (Table 6).

set.seed(1)
gaussian_density <- dnorm(0)
gaussian_cdf <- pnorm(1.96)
gaussian_quantile <- qnorm(0.975)
gaussian_draw <- rnorm(1)
binomial_mass <- dbinom(2, size = 3, prob = 1 / 2)
binomial_cdf <- pbinom(2, size = 3, prob = 1 / 2)
binomial_quantile <- qbinom(0.5, size = 3, prob = 1 / 2)
binomial_draw <- rbinom(1, size = 3, prob = 1 / 2)

call_text <- c(
  "dnorm(0)",
  "pnorm(1.96)",
  "qnorm(0.975)",
  "rnorm(1)",
  "dbinom(2, size = 3, prob = 1 / 2)",
  "pbinom(2, size = 3, prob = 1 / 2)",
  "qbinom(0.5, size = 3, prob = 1 / 2)",
  "rbinom(1, size = 3, prob = 1 / 2)"
)

call_values <- c(
  gaussian_density,
  gaussian_cdf,
  gaussian_quantile,
  gaussian_draw,
  binomial_mass,
  binomial_cdf,
  binomial_quantile,
  binomial_draw
)

calls <- dplyr::tibble(call = call_text, value = call_values)

knitr::kable(calls, digits = 4)

The value of dbinom(2, size = 3, prob = 1 / 2) is \(3/8 = 0.375\), which matches the two heads in three flips example.
